title: Saint Patrick (17 March)
hook: the breastplate prayer: Christ before me, Christ behind me

segments.voice: Yesterday, cathedra: a teacher's chair, a pun on rock, and your line, upon this rock. Who leaned on you, and did you hold? Day six hundred fifty-four.

Green rivers, green beer, plastic hats, a parade down Fifth Avenue. On March 17, people who have never been near Dublin wear green for a day. Ask someone at the parade who Saint Patrick was and you may hear: he drove the snakes out of Ireland and explained the Trinity with a shamrock. Both stories are later legends. In his own writing, Patrick never mentions a snake or a shamrock. The real Patrick left us something better than legends: his own words, and a prayer that carries his name.
screen: `GREEN RIVERS, GREEN BEER.` → `SNAKES AND SHAMROCKS.` → `HIS OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Patrick wasn't Irish. He was born in Britain, tradition says in the fifth century, the son of a deacon, a boy who by his own account didn't take faith very seriously. At about sixteen, raiders from Ireland seized him and sold him as a slave. For six years he herded animals on a cold hillside, and there, alone, he began to pray, he says, a hundred times a day and almost as many at night. Then he escaped, found a ship, and made it home. And years later, he went back. Back to the land of the people who had enslaved him, as a bishop, to spend his life among them. We know this because he wrote it down, in a short Latin work called the Confession, which opens with Patrick calling himself a sinner and very unlearned. No legend needed: the man tells you himself. Then there's the prayer. It's called the Breastplate, or the Deer's Cry, and tradition says Patrick sang it while walking past enemies who wanted him dead. It's written in Old Irish, and scholars who study that language place it after his lifetime; tradition gave it his name. Either way, it's a prayer of armor. It calls on the Trinity, then the strength of heaven, sun, fire, sea and rock. Then the famous part: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, beneath me, above me. And it ends looking outward, asking for Christ in the heart of everyone who thinks of me, and in every eye that sees me. A prayer that surrounds you, and then sees Christ in the faces around you.
screen: `A BRITISH BOY, ENSLAVED.` · `HE WENT BACK.` · `THE CONFESSION, IN LATIN.` · `THE BREASTPLATE, LATER.` · then, large: `CHRIST IN EVERY EYE THAT SEES ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the breastplate surround you. Sit, and breathe slowly. Then, with each breath, notice one direction: in front of you, behind you, to your right, to your left, below you, above you. If you pray, you can pray those old lines, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ beside me, one direction at a time. If you don't, simply feel the space around you and the people you'll meet today. Then think of the eyes that will see you, and the eyes you'll see. The bell holds the time.
Saint Patrick. A Briton, once enslaved in Ireland, who returned as its bishop; patron of Ireland, kept on March 17. Today's word.
Your line: christ in every eye. Today, look at three people's faces, really look, and see what the breastplate saw. Day six hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics keep March 17 as the feast of Saint Patrick, a solemnity and holy day in Ireland; some go to Mass before the parades, and the Breastplate prayer is sometimes sung as a hymn.

fork.setup: you're Patrick. you escaped slavery in Ireland and made it home to your family. years later, you dream of the Irish calling you back. what do you do?
options: go back to the land that enslaved you, as a bishop.
fork.reveal: he went back and spent his life among them. his Confession tells of a dream in which the Irish begged him to come and walk among them.

original.note: Latin: a breastplate; the name for prayers of protection like Saint Patrick's.

trapdoor: what you thought: Saint Patrick is about shamrocks and parades.
what it means: a Briton, enslaved in Ireland, who escaped and chose to go back as its bishop.
what a scholar hears: his Latin Confessio gives his own account, from capture at about sixteen to the dream that called him back; the Old Irish Breastplate was later given his name.

sources.work: Old Irish prayer attributed to Patrick

notes: The Breastplate is paraphrased and described, not quoted; its short phrases ('Christ with me, Christ before me...') are common to many translations. Confirm acceptable without a cited public-domain translation (e.g. Whitley Stokes, Kuno Meyer).
Dating of the Lorica (commonly 7th–8th century) and its traditional legend (Patrick and companions appearing as deer). Confirm.
Patrick's father Calpurnius, a deacon (Confessio 1); prayer 'a hundred times a day' (Confessio 16); dream of the Irish (Confessio 23). Confirm.
Snakes: Ireland has had no native snakes since the last Ice Age, per natural-history sources. Shamrock-Trinity legend first attested in the early 18th century. Confirm.
Saint Patrick's Day is a solemnity in Ireland and a memorial (optional when in Lent) in the general calendar. Confirm.
